opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what struck me most was how *curious* it was. At the time I was coming from a background that wasn't really in machine learning research. I'd been doing data science and was more on the applied side, so my mental model of neural networks was pretty much "you train it, you check the accuracy, and if the number goes up you're happy." And then here were Jason and Jeff treating these networks almost like a biological organism you could study. They were poking at individual neurons, visualizing what features they responded to, asking what the network had actually learned rather than just how well it performed.

That framing of it as "neuroscience," as opposed to just engineering, really reframed things for me. It suggested that these systems were objects worth understanding in their own right, and that there were genuine scientific mysteries inside them that we didn't have answers to yet. A lot of the questions they raised were things like: why does this work at all? What's going on in the intermediate representations? Those felt so much more open-ended and exciting than tuning a model for a business metric.

I think it was also the spirit of how they did research. It was playful and exploratory, willing to run an experiment just because you're curious what happens. That made research feel accessible to me in a way it hadn't before. It wasn't this gated thing where you needed to already know all the answers. You could just start asking good questions. That was a big part of what pulled me toward wanting to work with them and eventually toward doing research myself.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts judging networks by accuracy with unanswered questions about why they work and what their intermediate representations contain, clearly conveying strong performance alongside limited understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
So I was at Uber when Jason and Jeff gave that talk, and I remember being really struck by this framing of "AI neuroscience." The idea was basically: we're building these systems that work, that get impressive results, but we have almost no understanding of why they work. And instead of treating that as an engineering inconvenience, they were treating it as a scientific question, something you could actually poke at with experiments the way a neuroscientist pokes at a brain.

What got me was that they were showing these feature visualizations, these synthesized images that maximally activate a particular neuron in a network, and you could see that some neurons were clearly responding to things like fur texture or dog faces or whatever, and others were just... weird. Uninterpretable. And rather than hand-waving that away, they were asking, okay, what does it mean that the network found this useful? What's the structure here?

I think the thing that really stuck with me, though, was how much lower the barrier to entry felt than I expected. Neuroscientists have to deal with the fact that they can't record from every neuron, they can't rerun the exact same brain under a slightly different condition, they can't ablate things cleanly. We have all of that. We have full access. Every weight, every activation, and we can rerun things deterministically. So the mystery isn't that the information is hidden, it's that we just haven't figured out the right questions yet. That felt like an invitation. Like, this is a wide-open field and you don't need a wet lab to contribute, you just need curiosity and some compute.

And honestly, it changed what I wanted to work on. I'd been thinking about ML more from the "how do we get better numbers" side, and after that talk I started caring a lot more about the "what is this thing actually doing" side. That's a big part of why I ended up working on things like the lottery ticket hypothesis follow-up with Jason and Jeff, trying to understand what's really going on with those sparse subnetworks rather than just taking the result at face value.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts systems that achieve impressive results with researchers having “almost no understanding of why they work.”

astra-6.text: What struck me was the idea that you could study a neural network almost the way a neuroscientist studies the brain. You’ve trained this system, but that doesn’t mean you understand how it works. You can look at individual neurons, see what inputs activate them, and ask what representations have emerged. I found that perspective really compelling—the network itself becomes something you can investigate, rather than just something you measure by its performance.

r001.rationale: The response says that training a network does not mean understanding how it works and contrasts investigating it with measuring its performance. It does not clearly describe neural networks’ impressive performance or the field’s broader limited understanding.

sol-6.1.text: What struck me was the idea of studying neural networks the way neuroscientists study the brain: looking inside them and trying to understand what individual neurons respond to. We build these systems and train them, but that doesn’t automatically mean we understand how they work. That gap between being able to create something and being able to explain it is really fascinating to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between building and training neural networks and understanding how they work, but it does not communicate the contrast with their impressive performance.
